key_insight: The paper identifies a growing wave of suspicion that authors used generative AI in manuscripts, and shows this suspicion is rising faster than clear evidence or consistent editorial policies—risking unfair accusations and harm to scholarly communication.
problem_solved: Highlights and contextualizes the emerging challenge of unchecked generative-AI suspicion in academic publishing, revealing gaps in evidence, inconsistent publisher responses, and potential negative effects on authors and peer review.
method: Synthesis of documented incidents, editorials, and public discussions around suspected AI use in manuscripts.
Review and comparison of publisher and journal policies, guidance notes, and editorial practices related to generative AI.
Analysis of stakeholder responses (editors, authors, reviewers) to illustrate patterns, consequences, and policy gaps.
impact: Alerts AI/ML practitioners and publishers to the reputational and procedural risks of ungrounded AI-suspicion, motivating clearer guidelines, fair investigative practices, and education on responsible use and disclosure of generative tools.
visual_elements: Timeline of notable suspicion incidents and policy updates to show the recent acceleration.
Flowchart illustrating the accusation → investigation → outcome lifecycle and where harms can occur (false positives, career impact).
Comparative table/heatmap of journal/publisher AI policies (strict, permissive, ambiguous) to show heterogeneity.
Icon set depicting stakeholders (authors, editors, reviewers, publishers) and recommended best-practice actions (disclosure, evidence-based checks, appeals).
paper_title: On the troubling rise of generative AI suspicion in academic publishing
